prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
On April 11, 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying James Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise, a crew intended to make the third landing on the Moon, in the Fra Mauro highlands. Lovell was the most experienced astronaut then flying, a veteran of Gemini 7, Gemini 12 and Apollo 8, and Haise was a rookie who would have walked on the surface as lunar module pilot. Swigert was a late addition: the original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been grounded days before launch after he was exposed to German measles, and Swigert, who had trained as his backup, took his seat after only a few days of working with the rest of the crew. The launch itself went well enough, apart from the center engine of the second stage shutting down early, which the other engines compensated for by burning longer, and the spacecraft settled into the routine of the outbound coast, with the crew docking to the lunar module, which they had named Aquarius, and pulling it free of the spent third stage, while the command module they called Odyssey carried them toward the Moon.

The trouble had begun long before anyone aboard knew about it. Among the service module's equipment were two oxygen tanks, each with a heater, a pair of stirring fans and a thermostat to control the heater. The thermostats had been designed for the 28-volt supply used in the spacecraft but the ground power at the Cape ran at 65 volts, and a change in specification had never been carried through to the switches. During a countdown test a tank that would not drain properly was emptied by running its heaters for hours, and the high current fused the contacts of the thermostat shut, so that the heater could run unchecked, cooking the Teflon insulation on the wires inside the tank and leaving bare copper exposed. Nobody noticed, because the thermostat switch looked fine when it was checked and the tank was refilled and flown.

On the evening of April 13, about fifty-five hours into the flight and some 200,000 miles from home, mission control asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks, a routine request meant to keep the supercold contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch, and a few minutes later, at 9:08 p.m. Houston time, there was a bang and the spacecraft shuddered. A spark from the damaged wiring had ignited the insulation in oxygen tank 2, the pressurized pure oxygen fed the fire, and the tank ruptured, blowing off a panel of the service module and damaging the neighboring tank. Swigert's report, "Houston, we've had a problem," was repeated more calmly by Lovell a moment later, and for the next several minutes the crew and the controllers tried to make sense of readings that showed electrical power dropping, a master alarm sounding and the thrusters firing on their own. Looking out of a window, Lovell saw gas venting into space, which told him more than the instruments did: the oxygen that would have fed the fuel cells, supplied their electricity and water, and given them air to breathe was leaving the ship.

Within about an hour and a half the second tank was empty as well, and the command module was dying. The fuel cells needed the oxygen, so the batteries that were meant to carry the capsule only through reentry were all that remained to power it. The flight director, Gene Kranz, and his teams had to abandon the idea of a lunar landing almost at once, and the question became whether the men could get home at all. The crew shut down the command module to save what power it had left and moved into the lunar module, a spidery craft built to support two men for two days on the Moon, which would now have to support three for four, and which was in effect a lifeboat that happened to be attached to the stricken ship.

The route home posed its own difficulty. The spacecraft was on a free-return trajectory, which would swing it around the Moon and back toward Earth, but the course had been altered earlier to allow the landing at Fra Mauro, and it no longer passed close enough to Earth to guarantee a safe return. The big service module engine was no longer trustworthy after the explosion, so the controllers used the lunar module's descent engine, firing it for about thirty seconds soon after the crew had rounded the far side of the Moon, in a maneuver that put them on a path to splash down in the Pacific in about two days. After they came around the Moon, passing farther from Earth than any humans before or since, they fired the descent engine again, this time for a longer burn, to speed the return and bring splashdown forward to Friday, April 17.

Then came the problem of living through the trip. The lunar module drew on its own limited water and electricity, and the crew powered down almost everything, letting the cabin temperature fall to a little above freezing, where condensation dripped off the walls and sleep was nearly impossible. Haise developed a fever and a kidney infection, and the men drank far less water than they needed, which left them dehydrated and weak. Worse, the lithium hydroxide canisters that removed carbon dioxide from the cabin air were running out, and the supply in the lunar module was rated for two people, so that the level of the gas rose toward a dangerous point. The command module carried plenty of canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the items the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a suit hose and duct tape, and worked out a way to fit a square canister to a round opening, then read the instructions to the crew step by step, and the improvised adapter brought the carbon dioxide levels down.

There remained the matter of restarting the command module, which no one had ever powered up from cold in flight, with batteries that could not be recharged and with a margin that the engineers measured in amp-hours. Mattingly, the astronaut who had been taken off the crew, spent long days in the simulator in Houston working with the engineers to write a procedure that would bring the systems back in a sequence that would not drain the batteries before reentry. The lunar module also had to be used to correct the course once more, because the trajectory was drifting, and since the guidance platform had been shut down to save power, Lovell had to line up the spacecraft by hand, using the Earth's terminator as a reference to hold the attitude during a brief burn a few hours before reentry.

In the final hours the crew powered up the command module following Mattingly's procedure, jettisoned the service module and saw for the first time the extent of the damage, with an entire panel missing and the side of the ship scorched. They then released the lunar module, which had kept them alive and which would burn up in the atmosphere, and the three men in Odyssey prepared for the reentry. A radio blackout normally lasts about three minutes, but because of the shallow angle of the trajectory it ran longer, and in Houston the controllers waited through a silence that stretched beyond what they had expected, until at last Swigert's voice came through, and the capsule appeared under its parachutes. It splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa shortly after 1 p.m. Houston time on April 17, and the crew was picked up by the USS Iwo Jima.

The review board that followed traced the accident to the thermostats and the damage done to the wiring in the ground test, and NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks, removing the fans that had stirred the contents and the fragile insulation, adding a third tank and reworking the electrical systems. The flights resumed with Apollo 14 the following year. Lovell never walked on the Moon, and the mission was officially described as a successful failure, but the return of the crew became one of the best examples of what trained people on the ground and in the spacecraft can do when everything they planned for has gone wrong.
